paragraphs.text: Orgg is a red creature type used for cards that depict a Dominarian race of hybrids between Orcs and Ogres . Orggs are extremely powerful creatures with green skin, batlike ears, massive teeth, and two pairs of arms. They are also utterly dumb, though they can be trained.

There have only been four cards printed with the creature type Orgg. The first card to bear the type was Orgg ( Fallen Empires ) in 1994. According to Jim Lin , the idea for the card arose during a brainstorming session. The team wanted to create a big, stupid ogre that didn't know how powerful it was. The name comes from one of the original play-testers, Chris Page , who also did some design work. He used to call ogres "orggs", back when he was playing Dungeons & Dragons . It wasn't known if he just mispronounced it or if it was intentional, but the name stuck. The artist Daniel Gelon was asked to create "a cross between a goblin and an ogre; a mutant, basically. But when it attacked large monsters, it became a 'fraidy-cat."

The next Orgg, Trained Orgg appeared in Starter 1999 set, but was typed as a Beast for this beginner set. The last two Orggs were printed for the Judgment and Onslaught in 2002: Soulgorger Orgg and Butcher Orgg . Trained Orgg finally received the correct creature type in the Grand Creature Type Update of 2007 , though it was never printed as such. All Orggs are 6/6 creatures.
Similar to Vizzerdrix , the high cost vanilla creature Trained Orgg once was considered to be a " booster ruiner " by the community. Yet today, both cards are coveted in foil versions.

Despite having a reputation as a bad creature, the Fallen Empire Orgg has occasionally seen play at the highest competitive level of gameplay. Mark Justice included one copy in the Type II deck he used to become 1995 US Champion . Both he and future Magic Designer Henry Stern then made the semi-finals at the 1995 World Championships , with Stern choosing to play two Orgg s.

Reprinted into Fifth Edition , Orgg would next been seen at the top tables at 1997 World Championships . Kim Ju-Neon, a member of the Korean National team , was the sole undefeated player across seven rounds of Standard competition on Day 2. His " Big Red " deck included two copies.

Orggs are only known to have existed on Dominaria . On Sarpadia , Orggs were used in the war against Icatia by the goblin -orc alliance around AR 170. The Ironclaw Orcs veterans were a group of orcs that were extremely cowardly when it came to fighting their enemies, the Order of Leitbur . However, they were not dumb, often using goblins as kamikazes and genetic mutations to fight the Icatian Empire. They also had created the Orgg. Reod Dai killed one of them.
Much later, Twisted Experiment ( Urza's Destiny ) appears to show the creation of an Orgg by Gatha around 3863 AR, during the War with Phyrexia .
Orggs were also known to exist on Otaria around 4050 AR. It is possible that they were created by the Cabal to fight in their pits.

Orggs seem to originate in Magic , though similar creatures with similar names appear in other fantasy settings: e.g., Orogs ( Dungeons & Dragons ) , Orggs ( Clevatess ) , and Orgs ( Power Rangers ) .
For a while, Orggs were used as iconic creatures in marketing by Wizards of the Coast .

In 1998, an Orgg played a role in a Magic: The Gathering commercial, taking on "Bob from Accounting". Another add featured a Kezzerdrix and a Poodle Guy. To tie in to those, R&D made a simpler Orgg and Vizzerdrix for Starter 1999 , as the original cards were deemed too complicated for a beginner product. The commercial was also used for Portal , although there isn't an Orgg card in that set. Several versions of the commercial are known to exist.
In the Spring of 1999, Wizards of the Coast released a series of 9-inch action figures in a production run of 30,000. They included an Orgg with 6 points of articulation.
In 1999-2000, several Wizards of the Coast Game stores featured a statue of an Orgg as an eye-catcher.
